title: SPARK CSEC Physics - Paper 01 Practice Paper 5
subject: Physics
syllabus: CXC 22/G/SYLL 13, for examinations from May and June 2015
instructions: This test consists of 60 items. You will have 1 hour and 15 minutes to answer them.
In addition to this test booklet, you should have an answer sheet.
Each item in this test has four suggested answers lettered (A), (B), (C), (D). Read each item you are about to answer and decide which choice is best.
On your answer sheet, find the number which corresponds to your item and shade the space having the same letter as the answer you have chosen.
If you want to change your answer, erase it completely before you fill in your new choice.
When you are told to begin, turn the page and work as quickly and as carefully as you can. If you cannot answer an item, go on to the next one. You may return to that item later.
You may do any rough work in this booklet.
Figures are not necessarily drawn to scale.
You may use a silent, non-programmable calculator to answer items.

items.objective_statement: investigate the factors which might affect the period of a simple pendulum
items.stem: The period of a simple pendulum depends on the

misconception.label: Changing the mass of the bob leaves the period unchanged.

options.text: material the bob is made of

misconception.label: The material does not matter, only the length.

options.text: angle of swing, for any angle

misconception.label: For small angles the period does not depend on the angle; the relationship fails only for large swings.

steps: The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(l/g).
Only the length l and the gravitational field strength g appear in it.
So of the choices given, only the length changes the period.

items.objective_statement: express the result of a measurement or calculation to an appropriate number of significant figures
items.stem: A student measures a length as 4.5 cm with a metre rule. The number of significant figures in this reading is

misconception.label: The 5 is a measured digit and counts.
There is no third digit in the reading.
There is no fourth digit in the reading.

steps: Every digit actually measured counts as significant.
The reading 4.5 has the digits 4 and 5.
So it is quoted to two significant figures.

items.stem: Vernier calipers would be the most suitable instrument for measuring the

misconception.label: A bench is far longer than the calipers can open.

thickness of a sheet of paper

A volume of liquid is measured with a measuring cylinder.

items.objective_statement: distinguish between scalars and vectors and give examples of each
items.stem: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?

misconception.label: Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so it is a vector.
Displacement is distance in a stated direction, so it is a vector.
Weight is a force and acts downwards, so it is a vector.

steps: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.
Speed tells how fast without saying which way.
So speed is the scalar.

items.objective_statement: explain that a single vector is equivalent to two other vectors at right angles
items.stem: A single force may be replaced by two forces at right angles to each other. These two forces are called its

misconception.label: The resultant is the single force that replaces several, which is the opposite process.
A moment is the turning effect of a force.
A couple is a pair of equal opposite forces.

steps: Resolving a vector means replacing it with two perpendicular vectors that together have the same effect.
Those two vectors are its components.
Combining vectors into one is the reverse process and gives the resultant.

items.objective_statement: identify types of forces
items.stem: Which of the following is a non-contact force?

misconception.label: Friction acts where two surfaces are in contact.
Tension acts along a string that is touching the body.
The normal reaction acts where a body rests on a surface.

steps: A non-contact force acts through a distance without the bodies touching.
Gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic forces are the non-contact forces in the syllabus.
Friction, tension and reaction all require contact.

items.subtopic: Springs in series and in parallel
items.objective_statement: determine the weight of objects

stimulus.label: Items 7 and 8 refer to the following diagram, in which two identical springs support the same load in two different arrangements.
stimulus.alt: Two identical springs in arrangement X, side by side supporting one 1.0 newton load, and in arrangement Y, one below the other carrying the same 1.0 newton load.

items.stem: Each spring on its own extends 4 cm under a load of 1.0 N. The extension of arrangement X is

misconception.label: Assumed each spring carries the whole load, which is true of the series arrangement, not this one.
Added the two extensions, which applies to springs one below the other.
Doubled the series answer for no reason.

steps: In arrangement X the springs are side by side, so the 1.0 N is shared between them.
Each carries 0.5 N, which is half the load that gave 4 cm.
Extension is proportional to load, so each stretches 2 cm, and the bar they carry falls 2 cm.

items.objective_statement: determine the weight of objects

stimulus.label: Items 7 and 8 refer to the following diagram, in which two identical springs support the same load in two different arrangements.
stimulus.alt: Two identical springs in arrangement X, side by side supporting one 1.0 newton load, and in arrangement Y, one below the other carrying the same 1.0 newton load.

items.stem: Each spring on its own extends 4 cm under a load of 1.0 N. The extension of arrangement Y is

misconception.label: That is the parallel arrangement, where the load is shared.
That is the extension of one spring only; both are stretched.
Doubled twice over.

steps: In arrangement Y the springs are end to end, so the whole 1.0 N is carried by each in turn.
Each therefore extends by its full 4 cm.
The bottom of the lower spring drops by the sum of the two, which is 8 cm.

items.objective_statement: determine the weight of objects
items.stem: The weight of a body is

options.text: the quantity of matter in it

misconception.label: That is the mass of the body.

options.text: the force of gravity acting on it
the same everywhere in the universe

misconception.label: Weight depends on the gravitational field strength, which differs from place to place.
The kilogram is the unit of mass; weight is measured in newtons.

steps: Weight is a force, given by W = mg.
It depends on the gravitational field strength g at the place concerned.
So it is measured in newtons and is smaller on the Moon than on Earth.
solution.answer_line: the force of gravity acting on it

items.objective_statement: show how derived quantities and their related units are produced
items.stem: In terms of the base units, the newton is equivalent to

misconception.label: That is the unit of momentum.
That is the joule.
That is the pascal.

steps: Newton's second law gives F = ma.
Mass is in kilograms and acceleration in m s⁻².
So 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

stimulus.alt: A U-tube manometer with one limb connected to a gas supply and the other open to the air. The liquid stands higher in the open limb by a height h.

items.stem: The pressure of the gas supply is equal to

misconception.label: Gave only the excess pressure the manometer measures, not the pressure of the gas itself.
Subtracted the column, which would be right only if the liquid stood higher on the gas side.
Ignored the height difference, which is what the manometer is measuring.

steps: Take a level through the lower liquid surface, which is in the gas limb.
On the gas side the pressure at that level is the gas pressure.
On the open side it is atmospheric pressure plus the pressure of the column of height h above it, which is hρg.
The two are equal, so the gas pressure is atmospheric pressure + hρg.

items.objective_statement: determine the location of the centre of gravity of a body
items.stem: The centre of gravity of a body is the point at which

misconception.label: A body can be supported anywhere; the centre of gravity is where its weight acts.

options.text: all the forces on the body are zero

misconception.label: That describes equilibrium, not the centre of gravity.

options.text: the body has the greatest density

misconception.label: The centre of gravity does not have to lie where the material is densest, and for a ring it lies in empty space.

options.text: the whole weight of the body appears to act

steps: Every part of a body has weight, and all those weights act downwards.
Their combined effect is the same as a single force acting at one point.
That point is the centre of gravity.
solution.answer_line: the whole weight of the body appears to act

items.objective_statement: relate the stability of an object to the position of its centre of gravity and its weight
items.stem: A bus is made more stable by

misconception.label: Raising the centre of gravity makes it topple more easily.
A narrow base makes it less stable.
A taller bus has a higher centre of gravity.

steps: A body topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base.
The lower the centre of gravity, the further the body must tilt before that happens.
So lowering the centre of gravity increases stability.

items.objective_statement: use Newton's laws to explain dynamic systems
items.stem: A car travels at a constant velocity along a straight road. The resultant force on the car is

misconception.label: The weight is balanced by the normal reaction from the road.
A forward resultant force would make the car speed up.

options.text: opposite to the direction of motion

misconception.label: A backward resultant force would make the car slow down.

steps: Constant velocity means the speed and the direction are both unchanged.
So the acceleration is zero.
By F = ma, a zero acceleration means a zero resultant force: the driving force balances the resistive forces.

items.objective_statement: define energy
items.stem: Energy is best defined as

misconception.label: The rate of doing work is power, measured in watts rather than joules.

options.text: the force needed to move a body

misconception.label: Force is measured in newtons and is a different quantity.
Power is the rate at which a machine does work.

steps: Work is done when a force moves its point of application.
A body that can cause that to happen is said to have energy.
So energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules.

items.objective_statement: apply the relationship: work = force x displacement
items.stem: Work is done on a body when

misconception.label: A force alone does no work unless the body moves.

options.text: a force moves it in the direction of the force
it is held stationary against gravity

misconception.label: Holding a body still means no distance is moved, so no work is done on it.
Mass alone has nothing to do with work.

steps: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
If the distance is zero, the work done is zero however large the force.
So the body must move along the line of the force.
solution.answer_line: a force moves it in the direction of the force

items.objective_statement: define kinetic energy
items.stem: If the speed of a moving body is doubled, its kinetic energy is

misconception.label: A faster body has more kinetic energy, not less.
The kinetic energy clearly changes with speed.
Doubling would be correct only if Ek were proportional to v.

steps: Kinetic energy is given by Ek = ½mv².
Replacing v by 2v gives ½m(2v)² = ½m × 4v².
So the kinetic energy becomes four times as great.

items.objective_statement: differentiate between the caloric and kinetic theories of heat as they existed in the eighteenth century
items.stem: The caloric theory of heat treated heat as

options.text: the motion of the particles of a body

misconception.label: That is the kinetic theory, the rival view that replaced caloric.

options.text: a weightless fluid that flowed from hot bodies to cold ones
a form of light given out by hot bodies

misconception.label: Caloric was not thought of as light; a hot body glowing was a separate observation.

options.text: the pressure exerted by a gas on its container

misconception.label: Gas pressure is explained by the kinetic theory, not by caloric.

steps: The eighteenth century had two competing accounts of heat.
Caloric treated heat as a fluid substance that moved between bodies.
The kinetic theory treated it as particle motion, and that is the one experiment supported.
solution.answer_line: a weightless fluid that flowed from hot bodies to cold ones

items.objective_statement: differentiate between the caloric and kinetic theories of heat as they existed in the eighteenth century
items.stem: Which observation could NOT be explained by the caloric theory?

options.text: A hot drink cools when left standing

misconception.label: Caloric flowing out of the drink into the air explains this.

options.text: A metal spoon in hot soup becomes hot

misconception.label: Caloric flowing along the spoon explains this.

options.text: Rubbing two dry sticks together produces heat without limit
Ice melts when placed in warm water

misconception.label: Caloric flowing from the water into the ice explains this.

steps: Caloric was a conserved fluid, so it could be moved about but not created.
Friction makes heat for as long as the rubbing continues, with no limit.
That means heat is being generated, not merely transferred, which caloric cannot account for.
solution.answer_line: Rubbing two dry sticks together produces heat without limit

items.objective_statement: identify physical properties which vary with temperature and may be used as the basis for measuring temperature
items.stem: Which property would be LEAST suitable as the basis of a thermometer?

options.text: The volume of a fixed mass of liquid

misconception.label: Liquid expansion is the property a liquid in glass thermometer uses.

options.text: The pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume

misconception.label: Gas pressure is the property the constant volume gas thermometer uses.

options.text: The colour of a hot metal at low temperatures
The e.m.f. produced by a thermocouple

misconception.label: A thermocouple e.m.f. varies steadily with temperature and is widely used.

steps: A thermometric property must vary measurably over the range of interest.
Colour does not change at all until a metal is red hot.
So it is useless for ordinary temperatures.
solution.answer_line: The colour of a hot metal at low temperatures

items.stem: Which physical property is used to measure temperature in a resistance thermometer?

options.text: The length of a metal wire

misconception.label: The wire does expand, but the instrument reads resistance, not length.

options.text: The electrical resistance of a metal wire
The mass of a metal wire

misconception.label: Mass does not change with temperature.

options.text: The density of a metal wire

misconception.label: Density changes very slightly with expansion, but it is not what the instrument measures.

steps: A thermometer needs a property that varies reliably with temperature.
In a resistance thermometer that property is the electrical resistance of the wire.
The resistance is measured and read off against a calibration.
solution.answer_line: The electrical resistance of a metal wire

items.objective_statement: demonstrate that temperature remains constant during a phase change
items.stem: While a solid is melting at its melting point, the energy supplied to it

misconception.label: The temperature does not change during a phase change.

options.text: breaks the forces holding its particles in fixed positions
is stored as kinetic energy of the particles

misconception.label: The average kinetic energy does not rise, since the temperature is constant.

options.text: is reflected back to the surroundings

misconception.label: The energy is absorbed, not reflected.

steps: The temperature stays constant because the energy does work against the forces between the particles rather than speeding them up.
solution.answer_line: breaks the forces holding its particles in fixed positions

stimulus.label: Item 23 refers to the following diagram of three rods of different materials, each with a pin held on by wax, dipping into hot water.
stimulus.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 470 224" width="100%" style="max-width:460px;height:auto;color:inherit" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12"><path d="M56 96 L56 192 L96 192 L96 96" stroke-width="1.6"/><rect x="58" y="122" width="36" height="68" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.13" stroke="none"/><path d="M58 122 L94 122" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="76" y="212" text-anchor="middle" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">hot water</text><path d="M62 140 L384 140" stroke-width="2"/><text x="392" y="144" text-anchor="start" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">copper</text><circle cx="348" cy="149" r="5" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M348 153 L348 166" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M62 164 L384 164" stroke-width="2"/><text x="392" y="168" text-anchor="start" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">iron</text><circle cx="300" cy="173" r="5" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M300 177 L300 190" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M62 188 L384 188" stroke-width="2"/><text x="392" y="192" text-anchor="start" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">glass</text><circle cx="250" cy="197" r="5" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M250 201 L250 214" stroke-width="1"/><text x="300" y="84" text-anchor="middle" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">pins held on by wax</text></svg>
stimulus.alt: Three rods of copper, iron and glass dipping into hot water, each carrying a pin held on by a blob of wax at a different distance along the rod.

items.stem: The pins fall off in the order copper, iron, glass. This shows that

options.text: copper has the highest melting point

misconception.label: The melting point that matters here is the wax's, and it is the same on all three rods.

options.text: copper is the best conductor of the three
glass is the best conductor of the three

misconception.label: Glass is last, so it is the worst conductor of the three.

options.text: the wax on the copper rod was the thinnest

misconception.label: For a fair test the wax is the same on each rod; if it were not, the experiment would prove nothing.

steps: Energy travels along each rod from the hot water by conduction.
When it reaches the wax, the wax melts and the pin falls.
The copper pin falls first, so copper carried the energy along fastest and is the best conductor. Glass is last and is the worst.
solution.answer_line: copper is the best conductor of the three

items.objective_statement: explain the transfer of thermal energy by radiation
items.stem: Thermal radiation differs from conduction and convection in that thermal radiation

misconception.label: Radiation passes through transparent gases and a vacuum; conduction is the one that needs matter.

options.text: occurs only at very high temperatures

misconception.label: Every object at any temperature above absolute zero radiates.

options.text: carries energy from cold to hot

misconception.label: Net energy flow is always from hot to cold in all three methods.

steps: Conduction needs particles in contact; convection needs a fluid that can flow.
Radiation is an electromagnetic wave and needs no particles at all.
That is why it is the only one that can cross the empty space between the Sun and the Earth.

items.objective_statement: recall that good absorbers are good emitters
items.stem: Two identical cans of hot water are left to cool, one painted dull black and one polished silver. The can that cools faster is the

options.text: black one, because dull dark surfaces radiate well
silver one, because shiny surfaces radiate well

misconception.label: A shiny surface is a poor emitter; it reflects rather than radiates.

options.text: silver one, because it is a better conductor

misconception.label: Both cans are the same metal, so conduction through the wall is the same.

options.text: black one, because black paint is a good insulator

misconception.label: If the paint were a good insulator the can would cool more slowly, which is the opposite of what happens.

steps: Good absorbers of radiation are also good emitters.
A dull black surface absorbs almost all radiation falling on it, so it also emits strongly.
The black can therefore loses energy by radiation faster and cools first.
solution.answer_line: black one, because dull dark surfaces radiate well

items.objective_statement: differentiate between types of waves
items.stem: Which pair of quantities is transferred by a wave travelling through a medium?

misconception.label: Matter is not carried along; a cork on rippling water bobs but stays put.
If nothing were transferred there would be nothing to detect at the far end.
A wave certainly transfers energy; that is what makes it useful.

steps: Set a cork floating on water and send ripples past it.
The cork moves up and down as each ripple passes and stays in the same place.
The energy has travelled to the far side, the water has not.

items.stem: Violet light is deviated more than red light because in the glass violet light

options.text: travels more slowly than red light

misconception.label: Amplitude decides brightness, not the direction light is bent.
Violet has the shorter wavelength of the two.
Violet carries more energy per photon than red, and in any case that is not what sets the deviation.

steps: The amount a ray is bent depends on how much its speed changes at the boundary.
Glass slows violet light more than it slows red light.
The larger change of speed gives the larger deviation, so violet emerges furthest from the original direction.

items.stem: Ray N does not pass out into the air because its angle of incidence is

misconception.label: Below the critical angle the ray does pass out, as rays L and M show.

misconception.label: Ray M is the one grazing the surface, which is exactly the critical case.

items.objective_statement: illustrate the effect of converging and diverging lenses on a beam of parallel rays
items.stem: A parallel beam of light travelling along the principal axis of a converging lens

misconception.label: A parallel beam is bent by the lens; only the ray along the axis passes straight through.

options.text: is reflected back along the axis

misconception.label: A lens refracts light; it does not reflect the beam back.

options.text: spreads out as though from a point behind the lens

misconception.label: That is what a diverging lens does.

options.text: is brought to a point at the principal focus

steps: Each ray strikes the curved surface at a different angle and is refracted inwards.
The shape of the lens is such that all of them cross at one point.
That point is the principal focus, and its distance from the lens is the focal length.

items.stem: While the rod is held there, the leaf rises because

options.text: electrons are drawn up to the cap, leaving the stem and leaf positive
the whole electroscope has become positively charged

misconception.label: The electroscope as a whole is still uncharged; the charge has only been separated within it.

options.text: the leaf has been charged negatively by the rod

misconception.label: The leaf is left positive, not negative; the electrons move away from it.

options.text: the rod has touched the cap and passed on some of its charge

misconception.label: The rod is held above the cap and does not touch it, so nothing is transferred.

steps: The rod is positive, so it attracts the free electrons in the metal of the electroscope.
They move up the stem to the cap, which is nearest the rod.
The stem and the leaf are left short of electrons, so both are positive.
Like charges repel, so the leaf swings away from the stem.
solution.answer_line: electrons are drawn up to the cap, leaving the stem and leaf positive

items.objective_statement: distinguish between conductors and insulators
items.stem: An insulator differs from a conductor in that an insulator has

misconception.label: Every material is made of atoms.
The charges are there; they are simply not free to move.

options.text: very few charges free to move
a larger number of protons than electrons

misconception.label: An uncharged insulator has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

steps: A current is a flow of charge, so a material conducts only if it contains mobile charges.
In a metal some electrons are free to move through the lattice.
In an insulator every electron stays bound to its own atom, so almost none is free.
solution.answer_line: very few charges free to move

items.stem: One ampere is a rate of flow of charge of one

misconception.label: A joule per second is a watt, the unit of power.

Volts per second is not a named unit and is not current.

steps: Current is defined by I = Q / t.
Charge is in coulombs and time is in seconds.
So the ampere is one coulomb per second.

items.stem: A primary cell differs from a secondary cell in that a primary cell

Every cell works by a chemical reaction.

steps: A cell produces a current by a chemical reaction.

items.objective_statement: explain the concept of resistance
items.stem: The resistance of a component is a measure of how strongly it

misconception.label: Storing charge is what a capacitor does.
Current is not converted into voltage; the two are separate quantities related by the resistance.

options.text: increases the potential difference across it

misconception.label: The potential difference across a component is set by the supply and the rest of the circuit.

options.text: opposes the flow of current through it

steps: Resistance is defined as R = V / I.
For a fixed potential difference, a larger R gives a smaller current.
So resistance measures the opposition the component offers to the current.
solution.answer_line: opposes the flow of current through it

in parallel with the component whose current is wanted

The meter must carry that current itself, so it goes into the branch.

items.objective_statement: select a fuse or circuit breaker of suitable current rating for a given appliance
items.stem: The fuse fitted to an appliance should be rated

options.text: well below the appliance's normal working current

misconception.label: A fuse below the working current would blow in normal use.

options.text: as high as the supply cable will allow

misconception.label: A very high rating leaves the appliance unprotected.

options.text: exactly equal to the appliance's normal working current

misconception.label: A fuse exactly at the working current would blow on the ordinary surge when the appliance is switched on.

options.text: a little above the appliance's normal working current

steps: Work out the normal current from I = P / V.
Choose the next standard rating above it, so normal running and switch on surges are allowed.

items.stem: The output R is 0 only when

misconception.label: P = 0 is inverted to 1, so the OR gate gives 1.
Both of these make at least one OR input 1, so R is 1.
Q = 1 on its own makes the OR output 1.

steps: Work back from the OR gate: its output is 0 only when both its inputs are 0.
One input is Q, so Q must be 0.
The other is NOT P, so NOT P must be 0, which means P = 1.
R is 0 only for P = 1 with Q = 0.

items.objective_statement: identify the poles of a magnetic dipole
items.stem: A steel bar is suspended so that it can turn freely and it settles pointing north and south. The end pointing north is the bar's

misconception.label: The south pole is the end pointing towards the geographic south.
Both ends of a magnet are poles; neither is dead.
A neutral point is a place where fields cancel, not a part of a magnet.

steps: The Earth behaves as a large magnet, so a suspended magnet lines up with its field.
The end that seeks the north is named the north pole for that reason.
It is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic pole that lies near the geographic north.

items.stem: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by

options.text: increasing the current in the coil

misconception.label: Fewer turns give a weaker field.

steps: The field inside a solenoid depends on the current and the number of turns per metre.

items.objective_statement: identify the factors that affect the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
items.stem: The force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field is zero when the conductor is

options.text: at right angles to the field

misconception.label: At right angles the force is at its maximum.
A large current gives a large force, not zero.
The material of the conductor does not decide whether there is a force.

steps: The motor effect force depends on the angle between the current and the field.
It is largest at 90 degrees.
When the conductor lies along the field lines the angle is zero and so is the force.

options.text: a steady current flows through it

misconception.label: A steady current in the coil itself does not induce an e.m.f. in it.

options.text: it is held in a strong steady field

misconception.label: A steady field, however strong, induces nothing.

options.text: the magnetic flux through it changes

steps: Move a magnet into a coil and the galvanometer deflects; hold it still and the reading returns to zero.
The deflection appears only while the flux through the coil is changing.
So change of flux, not the flux itself, is what induces the e.m.f.

steps: Energy wasted in a cable is I squared R, so a small current is wanted.

items.stem: The electrons in an atom are held in their shells by

misconception.label: The strong nuclear force acts only inside the nucleus, over a very short range.

options.text: the electrostatic attraction of the nucleus

Electrons are negative, and unlike charges attract.
That electrostatic attraction is what binds each electron to the atom.

items.stem: Two isotopes of the same element differ in the number of

misconception.label: A different proton number would make it a different element.

steps: The element is fixed by the proton number Z.

steps: Alpha is a helium nucleus, so its charge is plus two.

items.objective_statement: describe the appearance of the tracks of radioactive emissions in a cloud chamber
items.stem: In a cloud chamber, gamma radiation produces

misconception.label: Thick straight tracks are made by alpha particles.
Tracks curve only when a magnetic field is applied, and gamma is uncharged so it would not curve at all.
Gamma does ionise a little, so faint tracks do appear.

steps: A cloud chamber track is a line of droplets condensed on ions.
The more strongly a radiation ionises, the denser the track.
Alpha gives thick short tracks, beta gives thinner twisting ones, and gamma, the weakest ioniser, gives only faint scattered wisps.

items.stem: The radiations X, Y and Z are, respectively,

misconception.label: A beta particle is far lighter than an alpha particle, so it is the one deflected the more, not the less.
Gamma carries no charge, so it cannot be the one bending towards the negative plate.
The undeflected radiation must be the uncharged one, and that is gamma, not beta.

steps: Gamma radiation is uncharged, so it passes straight through: that is Y.
Alpha is positive and is attracted to the negative plate, which is the lower one, so it bends downwards: that is X.
Beta is negative and bends towards the positive upper plate: that is Z. It bends far more because it is thousands of times lighter than an alpha particle.

items.objective_statement: use graphs of random decay to show that such processes have constant half-lives
items.stem: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for

options.text: half the sample to change into a different element by chemical means

misconception.label: Radioactive decay is a nuclear change, not a chemical one.

options.text: the sample to lose half its mass

misconception.label: The mass hardly changes; the atoms become atoms of another element but they are still there.

options.text: the number of undecayed nuclei in the sample to fall to half its value
the count rate to fall to zero

misconception.label: The count rate falls towards the background level but never reaches zero in a fixed time.

steps: Start with N undecayed nuclei.
After one half-life, N/2 remain; after two, N/4.
Since the activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, the count rate above background halves in the same time.
solution.answer_line: the number of undecayed nuclei in the sample to fall to half its value
